title: Keely Hodgkinson pulls out of Zurich Diamond League showdown with Audrey Werro
content:
Keely Hodgkinson has withdrawn from the women’s 800m at the Zurich Diamond League this Thursday, event organisers confirmed via email on Monday afternoon.

“Unfortunately, the body isn’t quite ready to race again after the European Championships, we’ve made the decision to skip this race and get ready for the next one,” the British athlete said in a statement provided by Weltklasse Zurich.

This means Hodgkinson misses the showdown with Swiss athlete Audrey Werro, who beat her to European gold in Birmingham, England, nine days ago, which prevented the 24-year-old from claiming her third straight continental outdoor title.

Hodgkinson, Olympic champion and sixth-fastest all-time, has battled with injuries throughout the past few years. Repeat hamstring issues limited her racing in 2025, though she still ran the second-fastest 800m of any woman last year (1:54.74s) and took bronze at the Tokyo World Championships off the back of only two races on the circuit that summer.

“I’m definitely a lot better than I was,” Hodgkinson told media about her fitness on July 17, ahead of the London Diamond League, where she won the 800m in 1:56.21s. In late June, a random fall during a cool-down — caused by tripping over the corner of metal floor meshing — resulted in knee injuries. “It wasn’t pretty at all,” Hodgkinson said in the pre-London press conference.

She still raced at the Prefontaine Classic in Eugene, Oregon, on July 4, and finished second in a time of 1:56.73s. “I did the best with what I could do. On reflection, I actually think it’s quite impressive,” Hodgkinson said. “Maybe I shouldn’t have ran but I definitely don’t regret it.” Lilian Odira beat her at Hayward Field, a repeat of the world championship final 10 months prior, when the Kenyan took gold ahead of Hodgkinson and her training partner, Georgia Hunter-Bell, the silver medallist.

Odira and Hunter-Bell are also scheduled to race the 800m in Zurich, as is Femke Broeders-Bol, the former world champion 400m hurdler. In her debut season over two laps the Dutchwoman took bronze at the European Championships and finished second behind Werro at the Lausanne Diamond League on Friday, setting a new national record time of 1:55.41s.

It is expected that Hodgkinson will compete at the Diamond League finals — hosted in Brussels at the start of September —with Werro, Broeders-Bol and Odira all part of the women’s 800m. One week after that is the inaugural edition of the World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, for which Hodgkinson (as Olympic champion), Odira (world champion) and Werro (based on world ranking) are all eligible.

It’s a real shame to not see another contest between Werro and Hodgkinson, considering how memorable their four meetings this year have been.

The first was back in February in Lievin, France, when Hodgkinson broke the world indoor record that had stood since her day of birth in 2002, running 1:54.87s, nearly a second quicker than the previous best mark. Werro, 22, was second that day, more than three seconds behind Hodgkinson, and those finishing positions repeated at world indoors in March as Hodgkinson added an indoor global title to her Olympic crown from 2024. Her 1:55.31s time won the race by more than a second, with the Briton bettering the 27-year-old championship record.

The outdoor season, though, has been dominated by Werro, who has won 12 times from 13 races this summer including Diamond League wins in Lausanne, Paris, Rabat and Stockholm. In the Swedish capital, she beat Hodgkinson for the first time thanks to her finishing kick, running 1:53.98s for victory — the third-fastest all time and the best performance for 43 years, since Jarmila Kratochvilova’s world record in 1983, which Werro is now within one second of (1:53.28s).

The crowning moment for Werro came in Birmingham when she demolished the European Championship record from 1982 to earn her first senior international gold medal, in the process handing Hodgkinson her first defeat in a continental final.
